Gamelan is the ensemble music of Indonesia, most prominently Java and Bali. It is built around metallophone percussion instruments made of bronze or iron, with bars struck by mallets. The ensemble creates shimmering, layered textures through interlocking rhythmic patterns and produces a tonal world foreign to Western ears, emphasizing different scales, timbral blending, and collective rather than individual virtuosity.

Gamelan ensembles vary in size, from ten to forty or more musicians, but always center on metallophones—slab percussion instruments struck with mallets that define melodic and rhythmic layers. The bonang consists of small kettle-gongs arranged in a frame, while the saron comprises bar metallophones with resonators. Together, these instruments outline the core melody, known as the balungan, while other instruments elaborate upon it to create the full texture.

Gamelan uses a five-note scale, creating an unfamiliar harmonic world that is distinctly Southeast Asian. The tuning varies by region and ensemble, with no universal standard pitch. This allows each gamelan to have its own sonic character and personality. The music accompanies dance, such as legong in Bali, shadow-puppet theater known as wayang kulit, and ceremonies. Performance is embedded in cultural and religious life rather than treated as autonomous art.

Rhythm in gamelan is cyclical and interlocking. No conductor is needed; musicians listen acutely to each other, creating a hypnotic effect through layers of repetition and subtle variation. The Balinese gamelan gong kebyar represents a twentieth-century innovation that is louder, faster, and more dramatic than the refined Javanese gamelan slendro, reflecting distinct aesthetic values between the two regions. Gamelan has influenced Western composers like Debussy and Satie, and modern world-music practitioners, through its collective aesthetics and tonal exoticism.
